A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MemoryVLA, with matching methods and identifiable corresponding experiments. All 30 pages of v1 and 36 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not constitute missing material.

before.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original simulation and real-robot evaluations, component ablations, and robustness experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds Mikasa-Robo experiments, further ablations, retrieval-attention analyses, inference measurements, and zero-shot task evaluations.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same VLM, perceptual-cognitive memory bank, temporal retrieval, gated fusion, adjacent-entry consolidation, and diffusion action expert. Additional dataloader explanations and experimental component variants do not establish a change to the proposed default method.

E1.justification: v2 adds five memory-dependent Mikasa-Robo tasks and zero-shot tests on three unseen object/target combinations relative to Apple To Basket. These extend evaluation beyond the retained SimplerEnv, LIBERO, real-robot, and visual-OOD coverage. LIBERO Long and LIBERO-90 becoming Long-10 and Long-90 is renaming, not additional coverage.

E2.justification: CronusVLA is added to the Bridge and LIBERO comparisons in Tables 1 and 3. The new Mikasa-Robo comparison includes OpenVLA-OFT and reproduced CronusVLA alongside existing comparator families. Appendix J additionally evaluates TTF-VLA and MAP-VLA on LIBERO, substantially broadening comparisons with temporal-context methods. TraceVLA, RoboVLMs, and 4D-VLA were already compared in v1.

E3.justification: New protocols include joint Mikasa-Robo training for 20k steps using 250 demonstrations per task and 128×128 observations, with 100 evaluation episodes per task. v2 also introduces five-trial zero-shot tests and inference benchmarking on RTX 4090 and HGX H20 in bfloat16. Section 4.2 changes Fractal's reported trial total from 2,352 to 2,856, but Appendix K.2 retains 2,352; an actual increase or rerun cannot be established.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Bridge ablations and OOD tests, Appendices E–I add retrieval-attention case studies, episode-length analysis, memory-length/fusion/consolidation ablations on LIBERO-90 and Clean Table & Count, a one-versus-four cognitive-token ablation, inference-overhead analysis, and zero-shot task generalization tests. These directly examine memory behavior and design choices beyond v1's ablation coverage.

E5.justification: Appendix H and Table 15 newly specify that inference measurements are averaged over 300 runs. Neither version reports training-seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests for task-success comparisons. This is a limited addition of repeated-measurement information.

E6.justification: Original MemoryVLA headline scores are retained, while v2 adds Mikasa-Robo results (41.2% versus PI-0's 29.4%), further ablation outcomes, runtime measurements, and zero-shot scores. Table 3 changes 4D-VLA's LIBERO average from 88.6 to 92.2, but v2 Table 17 retains 88.6 and gives CronusVLA 92.2 rather than Table 3's 86.2. The new claim of winning every Mikasa task conflicts with Table 4: MemoryVLA scores 24 versus PI-0's 42 on Intercept and 44 versus OpenVLA-OFT's 59 on Remember Color3.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and Equations 1–9 for actions, memory, retrieval, fusion, and consolidation are substantively unchanged. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations are introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and contribution list extend the performance claim to Mikasa-Robo, reporting 41.2% success and an 11.8-point advantage. The central methodological contributions and previous headline claims remain unchanged. The abstract also corrects the real-world aggregate's description from success rate to success score.

C2.justification: New appendix discussions substantially expand mechanism interpretation: attention to historical frames is interpreted as resolving current-frame ambiguity; episode lengths motivate larger temporal-task memory; cognitive-token results motivate a single-token capacity explanation; and compression/consolidation explain limited inference overhead. Appendix L further explains real-task memory dependence. The existing camera-view limitation and future-work discussion are retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds a reproducibility statement with explicit code, model, and log access links beyond v1's project-page pointer. It clarifies sequential and grouped dataloading, documents Mikasa-Robo data and training/evaluation settings, and specifies inference hardware, precision, and action-chunk configuration. These materially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to retained implementations.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Mikasa-Robo, CronusVLA, TTF-VLA, MAP-VLA, and several recent VLA works. Appendix J explicitly positions the results against contemporary temporal-context approaches. The original related-work narrative, cognitive-science motivation, and claimed perceptual/cognitive-memory distinction remain largely intact.

P1.justification: Most existing introduction, method, and conclusion prose is retained. Local revisions standardize LIBERO terminology, expand dataloader explanations, update the publication header, and add acknowledgments, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements. The appendices are reorganized and the qualitative sections combined, without a pervasive rewrite of retained content.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 4 are expanded for Mikasa-Robo; new Figures 10–12 visualize retrieval attention and memory-dependent ambiguities. Nine additional tables present benchmark comparisons, statistics, ablations, efficiency, and transfer results. Retained rollout figures are relocated and resized, including combining the SimplerEnv displays on one page. Figure 1 incorrectly labels Table 4's 28.4 OpenVLA-OFT result as π0-FAST.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central memory design: component testing extends beyond v1's Bridge tasks to temporal real-world and LIBERO tasks, complemented by a memory-focused benchmark, retrieval evidence, measured overhead, and explicit reproducibility links. These address important gaps in demonstrating where and how memory helps. New baseline inconsistencies, conflicting Fractal trial totals, and overstated Mikasa superiority reduce reporting reliability and require correction, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in direct validation and reproducibility.
